The great success of MLLM is inseparable from its compositional training paradigm, which independently pre-trains visual encoders [28] and LLMs [61], and then integrates them through additional multimodal training. Due to the engineering simplicity and effectiveness, this paradigm has dominated MLLM area over the past few years. However, the shortcomings of compositional training have been gradually recognized by the community recently, e.g., unclear multimodal scaling property [19, 56]. Therefore, increasing attention has been directed toward the development of more native MLLMs. As illustrated in Fig. 1, native MLLMs aim to jointly optimize both visual and language spaces in an end-to-end manner, thereby maximizing vision-language alignment. Compared to the compositional paradigm, existing native MLLM methods demonstrate a promising scaling law and a significantly simplified training process [9, 56]. Despite these advancements, the primary benefits of native MLLMs are often evaluated under the assumption of infinite training resources, overlooking the substantial challenges posed by limited data and large-scale training. Consequently, a critical practical question remains: whether and how native MLLMs can feasibly achieve or even surpass the performance upper bound of top-tier MLLMs at an acceptable cost. Figure 1: Comparison of design choices, scaling properties, and performance of our native MLLMs. We systematically investigate the designs and the scaling properties of native MLLMs under data constraints and yield valuable findings for building native MLLMs. After adopting these findings, our native MLLMs achieve competitive performance with top-tier MLLMs. \\mathcal { V } _ { d , w } ^ { * } ( \\cdot ) denotes the visual encoder with optimal parameter size. To answer this question, in this paper, we aim to systematically investigate the designs and the scaling properties of native MLLMs under data constraint. Specifically, we first explore the choices of key components in the native architecture including the mixture-of-experts, the visual encoder and the initialization of the LLM. Our findings can be summarized in two folds. Firstly, an appropriate pre-training initialization (e.g., the base LLM) of the LLM greatly benefits the training convergence on multimodal data. Secondly, combining visual encoder architectures and MoEs results in obvious gains against the vanilla decoder-only LLM. Following these findings, we build a meta architecture that optimally balances performance and training cost. Based on the optimal meta architecture, we further explore the scaling properties of the visual encoder, the LLM and the entire native MLLM. Specifically, we first scale up the LLM and the visual encoder independently and observe different scaling properties: while scaling LLM exhibits similar patterns as the conventional language scaling laws, scaling visual encoder shows an upper bound in return due to the limitation of the LLM’s capacity, suggesting that the optimal encoder size varies with the LLM size. Further analysis reveals that the optimal encoder size increases approximately proportionally with the LLM size in log scale. This observation yields a different guidance against compositional paradigm, which employs a visual encoder of one size across all LLM scales. Based on above principles, we propose a native MLLM called NaViL, combined with a simple and cost-effective recipe. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks to evaluate its multimodal capabilities including image captioning [10, 67, 2], optical character recognition (OCR) [57, 17, 39], etc. Experimental results reveal that with { \\sim } 6 0 0 \\mathbf { M } pretraining image-text pairs, NaViL achieves competitive performance compared to current top-tier compositional MLLMs, highlighting the great practicality and capabilities of NaViL. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We systematically explore the design space and the optimal choice in native MLLMs under data constraint, including the LLM initialization, the visual encoder and the MoEs, and draw three critical findings that greatly benefit the training of native MLLMs. • Based on above findings, we construct a novel native MLLM called NaViL. In NaViL, we explore the scaling properties of the visual encoder and the LLM and indicate their positively correlated scaling relationship. • We conduct large-scale pre-training and fine-tuning experiments on NaViL. Experimental results show that NaViL can achieve top-tier performance with nearly 600M pre-training data. Alternatively, initializing the model from a pre-trained LLM effectively leverages linguistic prior knowledge, significantly reducing data and computational demands. Fig. 10 further illustrates the difference between compositional MLLMs and native MLLMs. Compositional MLLMs typically have different components initialized by separate unimodal pre-training, where different training objectives and strategies are employed to train the LLM and visual encoder. For example, the visual encoder can be trained using an image-text contrastive learning objective (e.g., CLIP [52], SigLIP [72]) or a self-supervised learning objective (e.g., DINOv2 [51]). The complexity of such training process increases the difficulty of scalability. On the other hand, as discussed in [56], native MLLM optimizes both image and text modalities end-to-end using a unified training objective (i.e., next-token prediction (NTP)). This avoids introducing additional bias and significantly simplifies the scaling effort. # C More Related Works Research on Neural Scaling Laws. The foundational work on Neural Scaling Laws began in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain, where [29] established predictable power-law relationships demonstrating that performance loss ( L ) scales reliably with model size ( N ) and data size ( D ) , and that larger, decoder-only Transformer models are more compute-efficient. Following works [23] further extended such research to encoder-decoder architectures, observing consistency in scaling exponents on Neural Machine Translation (NMT) tasks. Driven by these successes, in the vision domain, [71] confirmed the applicability of scaling laws to Vision Transformers (ViT), systematically demonstrating continuous performance improvement by scaling both model size (up to 2 billion parameters) and training data. Most recently, these principles have been generalized to Large Multimodal Models, where [1] developed scaling laws that unify the contributions of text, image, and speech modalities by explicitly modeling synergy and competition as an additive term. Furthering this, [56] explored Native Multimodal Models (NMMs) using Mixture of Experts (MoEs), finding an unbalanced scaling law that suggests scaling training tokens ( D ) is more critical than scaling active parameters ( N ) as the compute budget grows. # D Implementation Details The hyperparameters of model architecture for NaViL-2B and NaViL-9B are listed in Tab. 6, while the hyperparameters of training recipe for NaViL-2B and NaViL-9B are provided in Tab. 7 and Tab. 8, respectively. ## Overview of the plan
# NaViL Reproduction Plan

## Overview

NaViL is a native Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) that jointly optimizes vision and language in an end-to-end manner using a unified Next-Token-Prediction objective. The paper's core contributions are: (1) systematic architecture design choices, (2) scaling law analysis for visual encoders and LLMs, and (3) a final model that achieves competitive performance with ~600M pretraining image-text pairs.

---

## Part 1: Architecture

### 1.1 Meta Architecture Components

The model has three main components:

**Visual Encoder**
- A stack of transformer layers with *bidirectional attention* (unlike the causal LLM)
- Uses 2D-RoPE for spatial position encoding
- Degenerates to a patch embedding layer when depth `d=0`
- Architecture formula: `V_{d,w}(I) = C ⊙ F_d^w ⊙ ... ⊙ F_1^w ⊙ P(I)`
  - `P`: Patch Embedding Layer (stride=16)
  - `F_i^w`: i-th transformer layer with hidden dim `w`
  - `C`: Connector (pixel shuffle downsampling + MLP projection)
- Parameter count approximation: `N ≈ 12 × d × w²`

**NaViL-2B Visual Encoder Specs (from Table 6):**
```
# Params:          0.6B
Depth (d):         24
Width (w):         1472
MLP width:         5888
# Attention heads: 23
```

**NaViL-9B Visual Encoder Specs:**
```
# Params:          1.2B
Depth (d):         32
Width (w):         1792
MLP width:         7168
# Attention heads: 28
```

**Connector**
- Pixel shuffle downsampling of encoded image embeddings
- MLP projection to LLM's feature space
- Input images padded so H and W are multiples of 32

**LLM with Modality-Specific MoE (MMoE)**

The LLM is extended with modality-specific experts. Each layer computes:

```
x_{i,m}^{l'} = x_{i,m}^{l-1} + MHA-MMoE(RMSNorm(x_{i,m}^{l-1}))
x_{i,m}^{l}  = x_{i,m}^{l'} + FFN-MMoE(RMSNorm(x_{i,m}^{l'}))
```

where `m ∈ {visual, linguistic}`.

**MHA-MMoE** uses modality-specific projection matrices:
```
Q_{i,m} = x_{i,m} W_Q^m
K_{i,m} = x_{i,m} W_K^m
V_{i,m} = x_{i,m} W_V^m
Output  = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V · W_O^m
```

**FFN-MMoE** uses modality-specific gating:
```
FFN-MMoE(x_{i,m}) = (SiLU(x_{i,m} W_gate^m) ⊙ x_{i,m} W_up^m) W_down^m
```

Key design: number of activated experts = 1 (no inference cost increase). Each token routes to either the visual or linguistic expert based on its modality token type, not a learned router — this is a hard routing scheme.

```
Depth:             24
```


### 1.2 Special Tokens

Four special tokens must be added to the tokenizer:
- `<begin_of_image>`: inserted before each image token subsequence
- `<end_of_image>`: inserted after each image token subsequence
- `<end_of_line>`: inserted at the end of each row of image tokens (spatial position)
- `<end_of_scale>`: inserted after each scale image in multi-scale packing

### 1.3 Visual Multi-Scale Packing

Given input image `I_0 ∈ R^{H_0 × W_0 × 3}` and downsampling rate `τ = √2/2 ≈ 0.707`:

```
Multi-scale sequence: {I_i} where H_i = τ^i · H_0, W_i = τ^i · W_0
Stop condition: area(I_i) < threshold
```

Each scale is processed separately by the visual encoder. The resulting token embeddings `{x_{i,v}}` are concatenated and fed to the LLM, with `<end_of_scale>` inserted after each scale's tokens.

**Unclear point:** The exact area threshold for stopping the downsampling is not specified. A reasonable default would be when the image area drops below the patch size squared (e.g., 16×16 = 256 pixels), or when the image is smaller than a single patch grid. This needs to be tuned or inferred from context.

### 1.4 Any-Resolution Support

Images are first padded to ensure H and W are multiples of 32. The model natively handles variable resolutions since the visual encoder uses 2D-RoPE and the token sequence length varies with image size.

## Part 3: Architecture Design Experiments (Ablations)

These experiments are needed to reproduce the paper's findings, not just the final model.

### 3.1 Experiment 1 — LLM Initialization (Sec. 3.2.1)

**Goal:** Show that LLM initialization converges 10x faster than training from scratch.

**Setup:**
- Base LLM: InternLM2-Base (1.8B)
- Visual encoder: fixed size (600M)
- Training data: web-scale noisy image-caption pairs (subset of Laion-2B / Coyo-700M)
- Two conditions:
  1. Model initialized from InternLM2-Base weights
  2. Model trained from scratch (random init)
- Metric 1: Validation teacher-forcing loss vs. number of training samples
- Metric 2: Zero-shot image captioning score (CIDEr or similar) vs. training samples

**Expected result:** Initialized model reaches same loss with ~10x less data.

### 3.2 Experiment 2 — MoE Effectiveness (Sec. 3.2.2)

**Goal:** Show MoE achieves same loss with 1/10 the data, no inference cost increase.

**Setup:**
- Base: InternLM2-Base (1.8B) + visual encoder (600M)
- Two conditions:
  1. Vanilla LLM (no MoE, shared FFN and attention for all tokens)
  2. MoE-extended LLM (modality-specific attention + FFN experts)
- Same training data and schedule
- Metric: Validation loss vs. training data size

**Key implementation detail:** The paper extends beyond Mono-InternVL's FFN-only MoE by also adding modality-specific attention projections (qkvo). This is the novel contribution — both MHA-MMoE and FFN-MMoE are modality-specific.

### 3.3 Experiment 3 — Visual Encoder Architecture (Sec. 3.2.3)

**Goal:** Find optimal depth/width ratio for a fixed parameter budget.

**Setup:**
- Fixed: LLM (InternLM2-Base, 1.8B), visual encoder total params = 600M
- Variable: depth `d ∈ {3, 6, 12, 24, 48}`, width `w` adjusted to maintain ~600M params
  - d=3  → w≈4096
  - d=6  → w≈2880
  - d=12 → w≈2048
  - d=24 → w≈1472
  - d=48 → w≈1024
- Metric 1: Validation loss vs. training data size
- Metric 2: Zero-shot captioning performance

**Expected result:** Moderate depth/width ratios perform best; shallower encoders converge faster early but deeper ones win with more data.

### 3.4 Experiment 4 — Scaling LLM Independently (Sec. 3.3.1)

**Goal:** Confirm LLM scaling follows standard language scaling law.

**Setup:**
- Fixed: visual encoder = 600M
- Variable: LLM size ∈ {0.5B, 1.8B, 7B}
- Metric: Validation loss vs. training data size (log-linear relationship expected)

### 3.5 Experiment 5 — Scaling Visual Encoder Independently (Sec. 3.3.1)

**Goal:** Show diminishing returns when scaling encoder with fixed LLM.

**Setup:**
- Fixed: LLM size (test with 0.5B, 1.8B, 7B separately)
- Variable: visual encoder size ∈ {75M, 150M, 300M, 600M, 1.2B, 2.4B}
- Metric: Validation loss vs. training data size

**Expected result:** Loss gap between encoder sizes narrows to near zero beyond a threshold.

### 3.6 Experiment 6 — Joint Scaling (Sec. 3.3.2)

**Goal:** Find the log-linear relationship between optimal encoder size and LLM size.

**Setup:**
- For each LLM size in {0.5B, 1.8B, 7B}, find the optimal encoder size
- Optimal encoder = smallest encoder where loss difference vs. 2x larger encoder < λ=1% of loss with 75M encoder
- Plot: log(optimal encoder size) vs. log(LLM size) — should be linear

**Unclear point:** The minimum area threshold for stopping multi-scale downsampling is not explicitly stated. A reasonable choice is `patch_size² = 256` (one patch) or `(patch_size * 2)² = 1024` (2×2 patches minimum).

### 5.5 LLM Initialization Strategy

- NaViL-2B: Load InternLM2-1.8B weights for all text parameters
- NaViL-9B: Load Qwen3-8B weights for all text parameters
- For MoE extension: initialize both visual and linguistic experts from the original LLM weights (copy the same weights to both experts initially)
- Visual encoder: random initialization (trained from scratch as part of native MLLM)
- MLP connector: random initialization

**Unclear point:** The exact boundary of "textual parameters" that remain frozen in S1.1 is ambiguous. The paper says "textual parameters of the model remain frozen, with only the newly-added vision-specific parameters being trainable." This suggests:
- Trainable in S1.1: visual encoder, MLP projector, MoE visual experts (W_Q^visual, W_K^visual, W_V^visual, W_O^visual, W_gate^visual, W_up^visual, W_down^visual)

## Part 6: Evaluation Setup

### 6.1 Inference Configuration

- Use greedy decoding for most benchmarks (standard practice)
- Visual multi-scale packing enabled during inference
- Images padded to multiples of 32 before processing
- Max image patches: 2457 (NaViL-2B S2 setting) during evaluation

### 6.2 Benchmark-Specific Notes

- **MME:** Sum perception score + cognition score; normalize to [0,100] for average
- **OCRBench:** Score out of 1000; normalize to [0,100] for average
- **DocVQA / InfoVQA:** Use ANLS (Average Normalized Levenshtein Similarity) metric
- **ChartQA:** Use relaxed accuracy (allow minor numerical differences)
- **ScienceQA:** Image-only subset (SQA-I)
- **CCBench:** Chinese cultural benchmark from MMBench paper

### 6.3 Evaluation Tools

- Use OpenCompass toolkit for NLP benchmarks (MMLU, CMMLU, MATH) — as stated in Table 5 footnote
- For multimodal benchmarks, use official evaluation scripts where available

## Part 7: Key Implementation Risks and Ambiguities

| Issue | Description | Suggested Resolution |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| MoE routing mechanism | Paper says hard routing by modality, but exact implementation of unified global attention with modality-specific projections needs careful indexing | Maintain a modality mask tensor throughout forward pass |
| Multi-scale packing threshold | Stopping criterion for downsampling not specified | Start with min_area = patch_size² = 256; ablate if needed |
| S1.2 data ratio | Exact split of 185M between multimodal and pure language not given | Use ~80/20 multimodal/language split as a starting point |
| Synthetic caption generation | 200M captions synthesized by InternVL-8B — requires running inference on 200M images | Use pre-existing synthetic caption datasets or run InternVL-8B inference offline |
| Pixel shuffle downsampling rate | The connector uses pixel shuffle but the exact downsampling factor is not stated | Use 2x downsampling (standard pixel shuffle factor) based on InternVL convention |
| Visual encoder attention head count | NaViL-2B uses 23 heads (unusual prime number) | Verify head_dim = 1472/23 ≈ 64; implement with explicit head_dim=64 |
| 2D-RoPE for visual encoder | Implementation details of 2D-RoPE not given | Follow standard 2D-RoPE from Qwen2-VL or InternVL implementations |
| Ablation model sizes | Exact LLM sizes for ablation experiments (0.5B, 1.8B, 7B) need matching base models | Use InternLM2-0.5B, InternLM2-1.8B, InternLM2-7B or equivalent |

## Part 8: Recommended Implementation Order

1. **Build the visual encoder** — bidirectional transformer with 2D-RoPE and configurable d/w
2. **Build the MoE-extended LLM** — extend InternLM2 with MHA-MMoE and FFN-MMoE layers
3. **Build the connector** — pixel shuffle + MLP
4. **Implement special token handling** — tokenizer extension and token insertion logic
5. **Implement multi-scale packing** — image preprocessing pipeline
6. **Implement the data pipeline** — multi-source loader with sampling ratios
7. **Implement the training loop** — stage management, parameter freezing, NTP loss
8. **Run ablation experiments** — reproduce Figs. 2–7 (design choices and scaling laws)
9. **Run full pre-training** — S1.1 → S1.2 with NaViL-2B
10. **Run supervised fine-tuning** — S2
11. **Evaluate on all benchmarks** — reproduce Tables 1, 2, 4, 5

This order minimizes wasted effort: validate each component before scaling up to full training.

## Logic Analysis: model/special_tokens.py

# Logic Analysis: model/special_tokens.py

## Purpose and Role in the System

`SpecialTokens` is the foundational token management class for NaViL. It defines and registers the four special tokens that encode the spatial and structural layout of visual content within the multimodal token sequence. Every other component that touches image tokens — `MultiScalePacking`, `ImagePreprocessor`, `NaViLDataset`, and `NaViLModel` — depends on this class to get consistent token IDs.

The class must be instantiated early (in `main.py`) and passed down to all dependent components. Token IDs are only valid after `register_with_tokenizer` has been called.

---

## Token Semantics (from the paper)

The paper defines four special tokens with specific structural roles:

| Token | String | Role |
|-------|--------|------|
| `BEGIN_IMAGE` | `<begin_of_image>` | Marks the start of an image's token subsequence |
| `END_IMAGE` | `<end_of_image>` | Marks the end of an image's token subsequence |
| `END_OF_LINE` | `<end_of_line>` | Inserted after each row of image tokens to encode spatial row position |
| `END_OF_SCALE` | `<end_of_scale>` | Inserted after each scale's tokens in multi-scale packing |

The insertion order (from the plan's "Shared Knowledge" section) is:
```
[begin_of_image]
  [scale_0_row_0_tokens] [end_of_line]
  [scale_0_row_1_tokens] [end_of_line]
  ...
  [end_of_scale]
  [scale_1_row_0_tokens] [end_of_line]
  ...
  [end_of_scale]
[end_of_image]
```

---

## Class Structure Analysis

### Constants

Four class-level string constants are defined. Using class-level constants (rather than instance attributes) allows other modules to reference them without instantiation, e.g., `SpecialTokens.BEGIN_IMAGE`. However, since the design specifies them as class attributes accessed via an instance, both approaches work — class-level is cleaner.

```
BEGIN_IMAGE  = "<begin_of_image>"
END_IMAGE    = "<end_of_image>"
END_OF_LINE  = "<end_of_line>"
END_OF_SCALE = "<end_of_scale>"
```

These strings must exactly match what gets added to the tokenizer. Any mismatch between the string used in `add_special_tokens` and the string used in `convert_tokens_to_ids` will result in the tokenizer returning the `<unk>` ID.

### `__init__`

Initializes `self.token_ids` as an empty dict. The dict will be keyed by token name strings (matching the constant names, e.g., `"BEGIN_IMAGE"`) and valued by integer token IDs. It is intentionally empty at construction time — IDs are only assigned after `register_with_tokenizer` is called.

No other initialization is needed. The class has no trainable parameters and no external dependencies beyond `transformers.PreTrainedTokenizer`.

### `register_with_tokenizer(tokenizer)`

This is the critical setup method. It must be called exactly once, before any component tries to use token IDs.

**Step 1 — Add tokens to tokenizer:**
```python
tokenizer.add_special_tokens({
    'additional_special_tokens': [
        self.BEGIN_IMAGE,
        self.END_IMAGE,
        self.END_OF_LINE,
        self.END_OF_SCALE
    ]
})
```

Using `additional_special_tokens` (not `special_tokens_map` keys like `bos_token`) is correct here because these tokens don't have a predefined semantic role in the HuggingFace tokenizer API — they are custom structural tokens. `add_special_tokens` returns the number of tokens actually added (0 if already present), which can be used for a sanity check.

**Step 2 — Populate `self.token_ids`:**
After adding, retrieve each token's integer ID:
```python
self.token_ids["BEGIN_IMAGE"]  = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(self.BEGIN_IMAGE)
self.token_ids["END_IMAGE"]    = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(self.END_IMAGE)
self.token_ids["END_OF_LINE"]  = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(self.END_OF_LINE)
self.token_ids["END_OF_SCALE"] = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(self.END_OF_SCALE)
```

**Step 3 — Validate IDs:**
After retrieval, each ID should be checked against the tokenizer's `unk_token_id`. If any ID equals `unk_token_id`, the token was not successfully registered — this is a hard error that should raise a `ValueError` immediately rather than silently producing wrong behavior downstream.

**Step 4 — Return updated tokenizer:**
The method returns the tokenizer so the caller can use it directly (e.g., `tokenizer = special_tokens.register_with_tokenizer(tokenizer)`). This is important because `NaViLModel.__init__` needs to call `llm.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer))` after registration to expand the embedding matrix for the new tokens.

### `get_token_id(name)`

Returns `self.token_ids[name]` where `name` is a string key like `"BEGIN_IMAGE"`. Should raise a `KeyError` with a descriptive message if the name is not found, and should raise a `RuntimeError` if `token_ids` is empty (i.e., `register_with_tokenizer` was never called).

---

## Key Design Decisions

**Why a dict keyed by name strings?**
The design uses `self.token_ids["BEGIN_IMAGE"]` rather than `self.begin_image_id` as a separate attribute. This makes `get_token_id(name)` a clean single-entry-point accessor and allows iteration over all token IDs when needed (e.g., for building modality masks that exclude special tokens from loss computation).

**Why not use `tokenizer.vocab` directly?**
`tokenizer.vocab` may not include newly added special tokens in all tokenizer implementations. `convert_tokens_to_ids` is the safe, API-stable way to retrieve IDs after `add_special_tokens`.

**Thread safety:**
The `token_ids` dict is populated once and then read-only. No locking is needed.

**Modality mask interaction:**
In `NaViLDataset._collate_fn` and `NaViLModel.build_multimodal_embeds`, the modality mask (`0` for visual, `1` for text) must treat these special tokens correctly. The four special tokens are structural markers inserted around visual content — they should be treated as **visual tokens** (modality=0) in the modality mask, since they are part of the image token subsequence and should route through the visual expert in `MoELayer`. This convention must be consistent across all components.

**NTP loss masking:**
In `training/loss.py`, the labels tensor uses `-100` to mask positions that should not contribute to loss. The special tokens themselves (especially `END_OF_LINE` and `END_OF_SCALE`) may or may not be included in the NTP loss depending on the training objective. The paper trains with NTP on the caption tokens, so image token positions (including these structural tokens) should be masked with `-100` in the labels. `SpecialTokens` provides the IDs needed to identify these positions during label construction in `NaViLDataset`.
